title: Near-miss incident report form for a small shop
summary: A one-page form that takes five minutes to fill out and catches the accident that has not happened yet. Template plus a fictional example entry.

blocks.title: Report the miss, not just the hit
blocks.body: A near-miss is the accident that got lucky: the sling that slipped without anyone under it, the chuck key left in the chuck, the guard found open. Small shops rarely have a safety department, so the form has to be short enough that a machinist will actually fill it out. Five minutes, one page, no blame. Everything below is a template with fictional example entries.

blocks.heading: The form - eight fields, that is all

items.label: 1. Date and time
items.detail: When it happened, not when you are writing. Example: 2026-03-12, about 14:30.

items.label: 2. Location or machine
items.detail: Specific enough to walk to. Example: Lathe 2, north end.

items.label: 3. What happened, in plain words
items.detail: Two or three sentences, no analysis yet. Example: Chuck key left in the chuck; lathe started and the key flew across the aisle and hit the wall.

items.label: 4. What almost happened
items.detail: The bad version. Example: Anyone walking the aisle could have been struck.

items.label: 5. Who was involved or nearby
items.detail: Names for follow-up, not for blame. Example: Operator at Lathe 2, one person passing.

items.label: 6. What allowed it
items.detail: The condition, not the person. Example: No spring-loaded chuck key on Lathe 2; shift was short-staffed and setup was rushed.

items.label: 7. What would prevent it
items.detail: The reporter's suggestion counts even if it is not adopted. Example: Self-ejecting chuck keys on all lathes.

items.label: 8. Reported by
items.detail: Name or anonymous - a shop that punishes reports stops getting them.

blocks.heading: A filled-out example (fictional)
blocks.body: Date: 2026-03-12, 14:30. Location: Lathe 2, north end. What happened: During a rushed setup the chuck key was left in the chuck. On spindle start the key ejected, crossed the aisle, and struck the wall about four feet up. What almost happened: the aisle is the main path to the tool crib - ten minutes earlier or later and someone is walking it. Involved: operator at Lathe 2; one person had passed a minute before. What allowed it: Lathe 2 has a plain chuck key, not a spring-loaded self-ejecting one; the job was a hot order and setup steps were being run from memory. Prevention suggested: fit self-ejecting keys to all three lathes, and add 'key out' as the last spoken word of the setup routine. Reported by: second-shift lead.

blocks.heading: What happens after a report lands
items: Same day: someone with authority reads it and decides if anything needs to be made safe right now.
Within a week: the report gets a one-line disposition - action taken, action planned, or reasoned no-action. Silence is what kills a reporting culture.
Monthly: read the pile as a set. Three near-misses around one machine is not three coincidences.
The fix gets verified: self-ejecting keys bought is not the same as self-ejecting keys installed.

blocks.title: Why a five-person shop needs this
blocks.body: Serious injuries are rare, which means there is little data to learn from - unless near-misses count. They are the free lessons: same causes, no ambulance. A shop that writes down its near-misses for a year owns a map of exactly where its next injury lives.

blocks.title: Two rules that make or break it
blocks.body: First: no blame, ever, or the reports stop and the map goes dark. Second: every report gets a visible answer, even when the answer is 'we are not changing this and here is why.' People will report into a system that listens; they will not report into a drawer.
